options.md: The fixed-length vector a model outputs for one input
options.why_md: Right.

options.md: The model that turns text into vectors
options.why_md: That's the embedding *model*. The embedding is its output.

options.md: The list of keywords found in a text
options.why_md: Embeddings capture meaning as numbers, not a list of keywords.

options.md: A vector with one number for each word of the text
options.why_md: Its length is fixed by the model, whatever the text's length.

hints: Separate the output from the thing that produces it.
The embedding model is the function; the embedding is the fixed-length vector it outputs.
solution_md: An embedding is the fixed-length vector an embedding model outputs for one input. The model is the function; the embedding is its output.

prompt_md: A 12-word question and a 300-word guide that answers it are embedded with one well-trained model. What do you expect?

options.md: Both vectors have the same number of dimensions, and their cosine is high compared with unrelated articles
options.why_md: Right. Fixed length, and similar meaning lands close.

options.md: The guide's vector has more dimensions, so it can hold more of the answer
options.why_md: Output length is fixed by the model, not by the text.

options.md: Their cosine is exactly 1, because they are about the same thing
options.why_md: Similar isn't identical. Expect a high score, not a perfect one.

options.md: Their cosine is low, because the texts share few words
options.why_md: Embeddings compare meaning, not shared words.

hints: Two facts: what decides the vectors' length, and what training does with similar meanings.
Same length (fixed by the model), and a cosine that is high compared with unrelated articles.
solution_md: Both vectors have the model's fixed number of dimensions, and because the guide answers the question, their cosine should be high compared with unrelated articles. Similar meaning, nearby vectors; not identical texts, so not exactly 1.

prompt_md: A question, *reset my password*, is embedded with model Q. The stored articles were embedded with model D. Both models output 768 numbers. The cosines come out as: billing article 0.93, password article −0.12, shipping article 0.40. What is the best explanation?

options.md: The question and articles were embedded by different models, so the scores carry no meaning
options.why_md: Right. A cross-model cosine is a number without meaning.

options.md: The billing article really is the best match for the question
options.why_md: 0.93 looks convincing, but it compares two unrelated coordinate systems.

options.md: The question is too short to embed well
options.why_md: Short questions embed fine. The scores are broken because two models are mixed.

options.md: The negative score proves the password article means the opposite of the question
options.why_md: No score here means anything: the two vectors come from different models.

hints: Before trusting any score, check which model produced each side.
Q and D have unrelated coordinate systems, so these cosines say nothing about meaning.
solution_md: The question and the articles come from different models, so the cosines carry no meaning: the billing article's 0.93 is an accident of two unrelated coordinate systems. Embed both sides with one model.

prompt_md: To save money, a team fine-tunes its embedding model on support tickets and uses the fine-tuned copy only for incoming questions. The articles keep their vectors from the original model. Both output the same number of dimensions. What happens?

options.md: Rankings become unreliable without any error: the fine-tuned copy has its own coordinate system, so using it means re-embedding the articles with it
options.why_md: Right. Fine-tuning makes a new model, and mixing models fails silently.

options.md: Results improve, because the question side now understands support tickets
options.why_md: Any improvement is wasted when questions and articles sit in different coordinate systems.

options.md: Nothing changes, because the architecture and the dimensions are the same
options.why_md: Same shape, different numbers: further training moved the coordinate system.

options.md: Search fails with an error at query time
options.why_md: The lengths match, so nothing errors. That's what makes this mistake dangerous.

hints: Does further training keep the original coordinate system?
A fine-tuned copy is a new model with its own coordinate system, so questions and articles are now mixed.
solution_md: Search quality breaks silently. Further training changes the coordinate system, so fine-tuned questions no longer line up with the original article vectors. Either re-embed the articles with the fine-tuned copy or keep the original model for questions.

prompt_md: Your model outputs 384 numbers per text. Which is a sound way to find the help-centre articles about billing?

options.md: Embed a few example billing questions and rank the articles by cosine against them
options.why_md: Right. Whole-vector comparison is where the meaning lives.

options.md: Find the model's billing dimension and sort the articles by it
options.why_md: There's no billing dimension. Single coordinates have no readable meaning.

options.md: Sort the articles by the sum of their 384 numbers
options.why_md: The sum of the coordinates says nothing about topic.

options.md: Look up which dimension covers billing in the model's documentation
options.why_md: No documentation can list it: training never assigns concepts to dimensions.

hints: Which methods rely on a single coordinate meaning something?
Only whole-vector comparison uses what the model was trained to get right.
solution_md: Compare whole vectors: embed a few example billing questions and rank the articles by cosine against them. No dimension is a billing feature, and summing coordinates measures nothing about topic.

prompt_md:
**Assertion (A):** Dimension 17 of a text embedding has a fixed human-readable meaning, such as *sport*, that holds for every text.

**Reason (R):** Training only rewards similar texts getting nearby whole vectors; it never assigns a human concept to a single dimension.

options.md: Both true; R explains A
options.why_md: A is false: no single dimension has a fixed, readable meaning.

options.md: Both true; R does not explain A
options.why_md: A is false, so 'both true' can't be right.

options.md: A true; R false
options.why_md: Reversed: A is false and R is true.

options.md: A false; R true
options.why_md: Right. R is true, and it's why A is false.

hints: Judge A and R separately before linking them.
R describes what training actually rewards. Given R, nothing gives dimension 17 a fixed meaning, so A is false.
solution_md: **d.** R is true: training rewards relationships between whole vectors and never names a dimension. A is false: a spun model would give identical results with a completely different dimension 17, so no fixed meaning can live there.
